newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: INTERVIEW-AIB sees strong Irish loan growth.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-AIB sees strong Irish loan growth.

text.p: Allied Irish Banks said on Tuesday that the lending environment in 1996 was very strong and it expected double digit lending growth in Ireland again this year.
Group financial director Kevin Kelly told Reuters that car finance and home mortgages in particular remained buoyant.

"In January, the car finance market was very strong. Car sales figures for January that came out a couple of days ago were even stronger than last January and home mortgages still seem to be strong," he said.
Although lending may not be as strong as in 1996, Kelly said the bank nonetheless expected double digit growth again.
Earlier, AIB announced a 13 percent increase in 1996 pre-tax profit to 421 million punts, above market forecasts.
"All divisions have done well and all business units within all divisions have done well," Kelly said.
AIB Bank, the retail division with operations in Ireland, Northern Ireland and Britain, saw overall loan growth of 14.6 percent last year.
Loans in the Republic of Ireland rose by 19.6 percent while Northern Ireland saw loan growth of 12.6 percent.
Lending in Britain rose by 7.1 percent while overall profits at AIB Bank rose by 15.7 percent to 226.5 million.
Net interest margins stabilised at 3.54 percent in the second half of the year but Kelly said they might only be taking a breather.
"It's still very, very competitive and I'd see some further decline in the year ahead," he said.

AIB said its capital markets division also did well, reporting a 14 percent rise in profits to 61.2 million, helped by the 1995 acquisition of UK fund manager John Govett which AIB said exceeded expectations.
Treasury profits were well ahead.
"They were very well positioned in terms of yield curves in a number of currencies and had a very good performance," Kelly said.
He confirmed AIB was planning to switch its bond market-making operations from Goodbody Stockbrokers to AIB Capital Markets as part of its preparations for Economic and monetary union (EMU).
"We are assuming that it will happen and that Ireland is going in. We are preparing very actively and we are providing for the cost of it as we go along."
The 1996 results included some provisions for the cost of converting to the euro, Kelly said, adding the bank was providing "a few million" each year for it.

Preparing for EMU, along with investments like AIB's direct banking operations and recent acquisitions such as Govett, First Washinton Bancorp and U.S. investment advisory firm Zirkin and Cutler, kept AIB's cost/income ratio at 64.5 percent, roughly the same as in 1995.
Kelly said the group would like to get it down to 60 percent by 1998/99 but its focus was as much on growing its revenue stream as on balancing costs.

The bank, which announced in January that it was acquiring Pennsylvania bank Dauphin Deposit Corp for $1.36 billion, said it will continue to review the acquisition situation while bedding down Dauphin.
"We have an open mind. If an oportunity arises we will look at it," Kelly said.
